newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan picks security boss to investigate killing.
newsitem.headline: Jordan picks security boss to investigate killing.

text.p: King Hussein appointed a veteran security figure on Friday to help unravel the motives behind the killing by a Jordanian soldier of seven Israeli schoolgirls, the state news agency said.

It said the king sent a letter to Mohammed Abdul Rasool al-Kailani, a veteran security chief who headed the powerful intelligence bureau in most of the 1960s and early 1970s, assigning him the task of directing the investigation into the causes behind the shooting by the lone border soldier on Thursday.

"My concern to uncover all the facts and dimensions behind this crime has prompted me to ask you to head and direct the affairs of the investigation in this crime," King Hussein said in a letter to Kailani broadcast by state media.
Kailani, 64, is a trusted confidant of the king who has also held the post of interior minister. His last post from 1993 until February 1996 was the king's national security advisor.
He told Reuters: "God willing I will achieve his Majesty's hope" in heading the investigation.

Officials confirmed that the gunman's full name was army driver Sergeant Ahmed Mousa Mustafa al-Daqamsa, born in 1971, from a small village called Idr in Jordan's Irbid province which overlooks northern Israel.

The Daqamsas are from the East Bank of the Jordan River, whose tribes are the bedrock of government support in a country of 4.2 million people of whom many are of Palestinian origin from the West Bank and Gaza.
The monarch has viewed the shooting as a personal attack on him, coming from the army establishment which takes place of pride in Jordanian society as his main power base.

"I am sure you share with me...and all members of the honourable Arab army's armed forces the feelings of pain, shock and shame over the vile crime...by the bullet of a treacherous coward, who has harmed the noble reputation of our army and its honour," the king told Kailani in the letter.
Political analysts say it is too early to say if the killing is a reflection of any disaffection within the loyalist army.

The king has insisted there was no political motive behind the shooting but officials say Kailani's choice is an tacit admission by the monarch of possible deeper political motives than just the said "vile criminal act."
"We assign you with this task and await the results of a thorough investigation into this crime," the king told Kailani.
The shooting took place on Jordanian sovereign land just south of the Sea of Galilee and leased to Israel under a 1994 peace treaty between the two countries.
The area is known to Israelis as the Island of Peace, but its leasing to Israel upset many Jordanians who saw it as perpetuating the presence of a former enemy on their territory.

Many Jordanians echo widespread disenchantment with the few tangible benefits from the peace treaty and accuse Israel of not wanting real peace with Arabs but being intent instead on seizing Palestinian land.
